opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the core issue is that prompting is fundamentally brittle. When you build an agent by hand-crafting prompts, you're essentially encoding your intentions into a long string of natural language and hoping the model interprets it the way you meant. That works surprisingly well for demos, but once you try to put something into production, you start hitting walls.

One problem is that prompts don't transfer well. You spend weeks tuning a prompt for one model, and then a new model comes out, or the provider updates the model behind the API, and suddenly the behavior shifts. All that tuning was implicitly fitted to quirks of a specific model, so you end up starting over.

Another issue is that prompting doesn't really scale with data. If you have thousands of examples of what good behavior looks like, there's only so much you can stuff into a context window. You can add a few few-shot examples, but you can't really learn from your whole dataset the way you could with training. So you're leaving a lot of signal on the table.

And then there's the composition problem. Agents are usually pipelines of multiple steps, retrieval, reasoning, tool calls, and each step has its own prompt. When something goes wrong, it's very hard to attribute the failure to a specific prompt, and changing one prompt can have ripple effects downstream. It's a bit like writing software without functions or tests, just tweaking strings and eyeballing outputs.

So what I've been excited about is moving from prompting to programming, treating the agent as a program with declared inputs and outputs, and then letting optimizers, or even fine-tuning and reinforcement learning, figure out the actual instructions or weights. That way you specify what you want, provide data and a metric, and the system improves itself rather than relying on someone manually wordsmithing prompts. I think that's the shift needed to make agents reliable.

r001.rationale: The response says optimizers can improve an agent using data and a metric, but does not identify the lack of a feedback loop from the agent’s outcomes as a limitation of prompting.

r002.rationale: It discusses prompt changes and downstream effects, but does not say that telling an agent its attempt failed is itself another prompt change.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the fundamental limitation is that prompting is basically trying to steer a model with English, and English is a pretty blunt instrument. You can get surprisingly far with it, which is why everyone starts there. But when you're building an agent that has to go through many steps, call tools, recover from errors, and do this reliably thousands of times a day, you start hitting a ceiling.

What happens in practice is you write a prompt, you look at the failures, and you add another sentence: "don't do this," "always check that," "if the user says X, do Y." And over time your prompt turns into this giant, brittle document that nobody fully understands. You fix one failure mode and you break two others, because the model is weighing all these instructions against each other and you have no real control over how it does that. It's whack-a-mole.

The other issue is that prompting doesn't actually teach the model anything about your specific environment. Your tools, your data, your edge cases, the particular way your users phrase things. The model only knows what fits in the context window, and it has to re-derive the right behavior from scratch on every single call. That's expensive, it's slow, and it's not very consistent.

So I see prompting as a great way to prototype. It tells you whether the task is even feasible. But I don't think it's a great way to get to a system that's robust in production. For that you need the model to actually learn from experience in your environment, from the trajectories it takes, from what worked and what didn't. That's really a training problem, not a prompting problem. And historically training has been hard enough that most teams just kept prompting, but I think that's changing, and that's where I think the interesting work is.

r001.rationale: The response says prompting does not teach the model from outcomes and that robust agents need to learn from trajectories, including what worked and what did not. This identifies the missing feedback loop.

r002.rationale: It describes reviewing failures and adding another prompt instruction, such as “don't do this” or “always check that.”

astra-6.text:
I think the main limitation is that, with prompting, you’re manually trying to specify the behavior you want. You look at a few examples, tweak the prompt, and it gets better on those examples—but you don’t necessarily know whether it got worse somewhere else. As the agent takes on more complex tasks, that process becomes difficult to manage.

What you really want is a way to learn from experience. If you can measure whether the agent did a good job, you should be able to use that feedback to improve it systematically, rather than having a human keep adding instructions to a prompt.

r001.rationale: The response identifies that prompting relies on manual instructions and contrasts it with using measured outcomes as feedback to improve the agent systematically.

r002.rationale: It does not observe that telling the agent an attempt failed is itself another prompt change.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the main limitation is that, with prompting, you’re essentially trying to describe the behavior you want rather than giving the agent a way to learn that behavior from experience. You can get something working pretty quickly, but then you see a failure, add another instruction, see another failure, and add another instruction. Pretty soon, you have this very complicated prompt, and it’s hard to know whether fixing one case has broken another.

For an agent that’s making a sequence of decisions, that becomes especially challenging. You want it to improve based on the outcomes of those decisions. Prompting is a useful starting point, but I don’t think manually refining prompts alone is a scalable way to get reliable agents.

r001.rationale: The response says prompting does not let the agent learn from experience and that agents should improve based on decision outcomes, identifying the missing feedback loop.

r002.rationale: It describes seeing a failure and adding another instruction, conveying that communicating a failure is handled through another prompt change.
